related_questions.question: What does an RA flare feel like?

text_blocks.snippet: An RA flare feels like a sudden and significant increase in rheumatoid arthritis symptoms, often involving intense joint pain, swelling, and stiffness. These flares can also bring about extreme fatigue, flu-like symptoms, and a general feeling of unwellness.
snippet_highlighted_words: a sudden and significant increase in rheumatoid arthritis symptoms, often involving intense joint pain, swelling, and stiffness

list.title: Joint Pain and Swelling:
list.snippet: A primary characteristic of an RA flare is a noticeable increase in pain, sometimes described as bone-deep, and swelling in the joints. This can make even simple movements difficult.

list.title: Stiffness:
list.snippet: Stiffness, particularly in the morning or after periods of inactivity, is another common symptom. It can feel as if the joints have "rusted" overnight.

list.title: Fatigue:
list.snippet: Extreme fatigue, which can be debilitating, is a hallmark of RA flares. This fatigue can be so severe that it interferes with daily activities.

list.title: Flu-like Symptoms:
list.snippet: Some people experience flu-like symptoms during a flare, such as fever, chills, and general malaise.

list.title: Other Possible Symptoms:
list.snippet: Depending on the individual, RA flares can also include anxiety, mood changes, and even symptoms like difficulty breathing, numbness, tingling, or disrupted sleep.

text_blocks.snippet: In essence, an RA flare can make it feel like your body is fighting a bad flu while simultaneously having your joints severely inflamed and painful. The severity and duration of flares vary, but they can significantly impact daily life. It's important to work with a rheumatologist to manage symptoms and potentially reduce the frequency and intensity of flares.

related_questions.question: What is the best thing to do for rheumatoid arthritis?

text_blocks.snippet: The best course of action for rheumatoid arthritis involves a combination of medical treatment, lifestyle adjustments, and self-care practices. Medications, including disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) and biologics, are crucial for managing inflammation and slowing disease progression. Lifestyle changes like exercise, a healthy diet, stress management, and physical therapy can further improve symptoms and overall well-being.
snippet_highlighted_words: a combination of medical treatment, lifestyle adjustments, and self-care practices

list.title: DMARDs (Disease-Modifying Antirheumatic Drugs):
list.snippet: These medications, such as methotrexate, hydroxychloroquine, and sulfasalazine, are often the first line of treatment to reduce inflammation and prevent joint damage.

list.title: Biologics:
list.snippet: These newer medications target specific parts of the immune system to reduce inflammation and are often used when DMARDs are not enough.

list.title: NSAIDs (Nonsteroidal Anti-inflammatory Drugs):
list.snippet: NSAIDs like ibuprofen and naproxen can help with pain and inflammation, but they do not slow down the progression of the disease.

list.title: Corticosteroids:
list.snippet: Medications like prednisone can provide quick relief from pain and inflammation, but long-term use can have side effects, so they are often used to manage flares or bridge the gap while other treatments take effect.

list.title: Exercise:
list.snippet: Regular, low-impact exercise can improve joint flexibility, strength, and overall physical function.

list.title: Diet:
list.snippet: A healthy diet, particularly one rich in fruits, vegetables, and omega-3 fatty acids, can help manage inflammation and improve overall health.

list.title: Stress Management:
list.snippet: Techniques like deep breathing, meditation, and mindfulness can help reduce stress, which can worsen RA symptoms.

list.title: Physical Therapy:
list.snippet: Physical therapists can provide tailored exercise programs, teach joint protection techniques, and help manage pain.

list.title: Smoking Cessation:
list.snippet: Smoking can worsen RA symptoms and increase the risk of complications.

list.title: Rest and Activity Balance:
list.snippet: It's important to balance periods of rest with physical activity, especially during flares.

list.title: Heat and Cold Therapy:
list.snippet: Applying heat or cold to affected joints can help relieve pain and stiffness.

list.title: Joint Protection:
list.snippet: Using assistive devices, pacing activities, and modifying tasks can help protect joints from further damage.

list.title: Education and Support:
list.snippet: Learning about RA and joining support groups can help individuals cope with the challenges of living with the condition.

text_blocks.snippet: It's crucial to work closely with a healthcare professional to develop a personalized treatment plan that addresses individual needs and preferences.

related_questions.question: How quickly does rheumatoid arthritis spread?

text_blocks.snippet: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) progression varies significantly between individuals, but it generally has a gradual onset, developing over weeks or months, according to the NHS. While some cases can progress rapidly over days, this is less common. The disease can also fluctuate, with periods of active symptoms (flares) and periods of remission where symptoms are less noticeable.
snippet_highlighted_words: generally has a gradual onset, developing over weeks or months

list.title: Gradual Onset:
list.snippet: The typical RA progression involves a slow development of symptoms, such as joint pain, stiffness, and swelling, over several weeks or months, according to the Johns Hopkins Arthritis Center.

list.title: Rapid Onset (Less Common):
list.snippet: In some cases, RA can manifest more quickly, with symptoms developing over a few days.

list.title: Fluctuating Course:
list.snippet: RA is characterized by periods of active disease (flares) and periods of remission, where symptoms are less severe or absent.

list.title: Symmetric Involvement:
list.snippet: RA tends to affect joints on both sides of the body (symmetrically), initially often involving smaller joints like those in the hands and feet, according to Mount Sinai.

list.title: Progressive Nature:
list.snippet: If left untreated, RA can lead to joint damage, including cartilage and bone erosion.

list.title: Individual Variability:
list.snippet: The speed and severity of RA progression differ greatly from person to person. Some individuals may experience a slow, gradual progression over many years, while others may have a more rapid course.

text_blocks.snippet: Relationship between Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA) and COVID-19
Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and COVID-19 share certain inflammatory pathways, which may increase the risk and severity of COVID-19 infection in individuals with RA.
snippet_highlighted_words: may increase the risk and severity of COVID-19 infection in individuals with RA

list.snippet: RA patients have a weakened immune system due to immunosuppressant medications and chronic inflammation.
This increases their susceptibility to viral infections, including COVID-19.
RA patients may experience more severe symptoms of COVID-19, such as:
Persistent fever
Lung complications (pneumonia)
Cytokine storm (overactive immune response)

list.title: Medications:
list.snippet: Certain RA medications, such as corticosteroids and biologics, can suppress the immune system and increase the risk of COVID-19.

list.title: Comorbidities:
list.snippet: RA patients often have other underlying health conditions, such as heart disease and diabetes, which can also increase their COVID-19 risk.

list.title: Joint Involvement:
list.snippet: RA patients with active joint inflammation may have difficulty with daily activities, including wearing a mask and hand hygiene.
Vaccination: RA patients should get vaccinated against COVID-19 as soon as possible.
Mask-wearing and Social Distancing: Adhering to public health measures is crucial for reducing infection risk.
Medications: Patients should discuss their RA medications with their healthcare provider to ensure they are taking appropriate precautions.
Monitoring Symptoms: RA patients should monitor their symptoms closely and seek medical attention promptly if they develop any signs of COVID-19.

text_blocks.snippet: RA patients have an increased risk of developing severe COVID-19 due to their weakened immune system and chronic inflammation. It is important for RA patients to take appropriate precautions and consult their healthcare provider for proper management and prevention.
